subject: Davidic census numbers, plague duration option, and threshing floor purchase price

figures.name: Israel's fighting men (census total)
figures.note: MT 2 Sam 24:9 reports 800,000 valiant men of Israel; LXX (Vaticanus) reads 900,000; 1 Chronicles 21:5 MT gives 1,100,000, showing internal biblical divergence as well.

figures.name: Judah's fighting men (census total)
figures.note: MT and LXX agree on 500,000 in 2 Samuel; the Chronicles parallel gives 470,000, again pointing to internal divergence rather than MT/LXX split.

figures.name: Years of famine offered as judgment
figures.note: MT 2 Sam 24:13 offers seven years of famine; LXX reads three years, harmonizing with 1 Chronicles 21:12 MT.

figures.name: Price of Araunah's threshing floor and oxen (shekels of silver)
figures.note: MT and LXX agree on 50 shekels of silver in 2 Sam 24:24; the Chronicles parallel (1 Chr 21:25) reports 600 shekels of gold for the broader site.

figures.name: Days of plague
figures.note: Both MT and LXX agree on three days of pestilence.

figures.name: Plague casualties
figures.note: MT and LXX agree on 70,000 men dying; Chronicles concurs.

systematic_analysis.pattern: The Samaritan Pentateuch is irrelevant here since 2 Samuel lies outside the Pentateuch. The principal divergences are between MT 2 Samuel, LXX 2 Samuel (Kingdoms), and the parallel MT/LXX of 1 Chronicles 21. The LXX of 2 Samuel 24:13 reads 'three years' against MT's 'seven,' clearly harmonizing toward Chronicles, while the Israel census figure shows three competing numbers (MT Sam 800k, LXX Sam 900k, Chr 1.1M) with no clean arithmetic rule linking them.
systematic_analysis.pattern_plain: There isn't a tidy mathematical pattern here—just a cluster of conflicting numbers between Samuel and Chronicles, with the Greek translators tending to smooth out the famine figure to match Chronicles. The Samaritan Pentateuch doesn't apply because this passage isn't in the Torah.

theories.name: LXX harmonization toward Chronicles
theories.summary: The LXX reading of 'three years' famine in 2 Sam 24:13 against MT's 'seven' is widely judged a secondary harmonization to the parallel in 1 Chr 21:12, which also reads three. This is a classic case where the shorter, harder MT reading (lectio difficilior) is preferred, and the LXX shows the translator or Vorlage smoothing a perceived contradiction.
theories.summary_plain: The Greek version probably changed 'seven years' to 'three years' so it would match the version of the same story in 1 Chronicles. Most scholars see the Hebrew's 'seven' as the older, harder reading.
supporting_evidence: 1 Chronicles 21:12 reads three years in both MT and LXX, providing an obvious harmonization target.
The principle of lectio difficilior favors MT's 'seven,' since a scribe is more likely to reduce than to expand the divine threat.
4QSam-a fragments and Josephus (Ant. 7.321) align with the 'seven' tradition in places, suggesting the LXX divergence is translational/secondary.
LXX Kingdoms is known elsewhere to harmonize Samuel-Kings figures with Chronicles.
weaknesses: Some scholars (e.g., McCarter) argue the LXX preserves an older reading and that MT 'seven' is itself a scribal error influenced by the seven-year famine motif (cf. Gen 41; 2 Kgs 8:1).
The 800k/900k census divergence cannot be explained purely as harmonization, since neither matches Chronicles' 1,100,000.

theories.name: Scribal error in numerical transmission
theories.summary: The census discrepancies (Sam MT 800k/500k vs. Chr 1.1M/470k; LXX Sam 900k) plausibly reflect copying errors involving Hebrew numeral letters or alphabetic numerals, which are notoriously unstable in transmission. Klein, McCarter, and others note that large round numbers in Samuel-Kings/Chronicles parallels routinely diverge in ways consistent with confusion of אלף (thousand) with similar graphemes or with abbreviated numeral signs.
theories.summary_plain: Big round numbers in ancient Hebrew were easy to miscopy, and the differences between Samuel, Chronicles, and the Greek look like the kinds of mistakes scribes typically made. No single deliberate scheme accounts for all the variants.
supporting_evidence: Numerical variants between Samuel and Chronicles are pervasive (e.g., 2 Sam 8:4 vs. 1 Chr 18:4; 2 Sam 10:18 vs. 1 Chr 19:18) and lack systematic direction.
The 800k/900k Sam variant is exactly the kind of single-digit numeral confusion expected in transmission.
Qumran Samuel manuscripts confirm that numerical readings in Samuel were fluid in the late Second Temple period.
No theological motive cleanly explains why Israel's count would shrink while Judah's stays constant.
weaknesses: Pure scribal error does not explain the directional 7→3 famine harmonization in LXX, which looks intentional.
Some divergences (e.g., Araunah's 50 silver vs. Ornan's 600 gold) are too large and category-shifted for simple miscopy.

theories.name: Independent textual traditions behind Samuel and Chronicles
theories.summary: The 2 Samuel 24 // 1 Chronicles 21 divergences may reflect that the Chronicler used a Vorlage of Samuel different from proto-MT, possibly closer to 4QSam-a, and that LXX 2 Kingdoms drew on yet another Hebrew text-type. This 'multiple Hebrew editions' model (Cross, Ulrich, Tov) sees the variants as inherited rather than created at the translation stage.
theories.summary_plain: Different ancient Hebrew copies of Samuel circulated with different numbers, and Chronicles and the Greek translation each used a different one. So the differences may be older than any single copying mistake.
supporting_evidence: 4QSam-a frequently agrees with LXX against MT, demonstrating multiple Hebrew text-types for Samuel.
The Chronicler's Vorlage of Samuel is known to differ from proto-MT in numerous places.
Frank Moore Cross's local-texts theory accommodates the Samuel/Kingdoms numerical variants well.
The Araunah/Ornan price difference (50 silver vs. 600 gold) may reflect distinct source traditions, not error.
weaknesses: This theory describes the situation more than it explains the specific direction of changes.
Some LXX variants (like the famine figure) still look like translator-level harmonization rather than Vorlage difference.

theories.name: Theological motivation in number selection
theories.summary: Some have argued that the differing prices (50 silver in Sam vs. 600 gold in Chr) reflect the Chronicler's elevated theology of the Temple site, and that the seven-year famine in MT reflects a covenant-curse schema (cf. Lev 26). Theological shaping is plausible at the compositional level for Chronicles but is hard to demonstrate for the LXX/MT differences in Samuel itself.
theories.summary_plain: Some of the number changes might reflect the writers' religious priorities—especially Chronicles inflating the Temple site's purchase price to dignify it. But this doesn't explain most of the smaller differences.
supporting_evidence: 1 Chr 21:25 raises the price to 600 shekels of gold, fitting Chronicles' Temple-centered agenda.
MT's 'seven years' aligns with covenantal curse patterns familiar from Leviticus and 2 Kings 8:1.
The Chronicler systematically reshapes Davidic material toward cultic concerns.
weaknesses: No clear theological motive explains the 800k/900k Israel census variant.
Theological motivation is often invoked when evidence is thin and is hard to falsify.
The plague casualties (70,000) and duration (3 days) show no theological reshaping despite being prime candidates.

theories.name: MT deflation of figures
theories.summary: One could argue MT 2 Samuel deflates the Israel census (800k) relative to LXX (900k) and Chronicles (1.1M), but the pattern is not systematic and the famine figure runs the opposite direction (MT 7 > LXX 3). There is no coherent deflationary scheme in this chapter comparable to the antediluvian chronology debate.
theories.summary_plain: There's no real evidence the Hebrew text systematically shrunk the numbers here—if anything, MT has the larger famine number.
supporting_evidence: MT's 800k is lower than both LXX (900k) and Chronicles (1.1M) for Israel's census.
Sexton-style arguments for MT deflation elsewhere (Genesis 5/11) raise the question for other passages.
weaknesses: MT's seven-year famine is larger, not smaller, than LXX's three years—directly contradicting deflation.
MT and LXX agree on Judah (500k), plague deaths (70k), and price (50 shekels), leaving no consistent pattern.
The Genesis 5/11 deflation arguments do not transfer to narrative books with different transmission profiles.

theories.name: Samaritan Pentateuch harmonization
theories.summary: The Samaritan Pentateuch contains only the Torah (Genesis–Deuteronomy) and therefore has no text of 2 Samuel. This theory is categorically inapplicable to the present passage.
theories.summary_plain: The Samaritan Bible only includes the first five books, so it has nothing to say about 2 Samuel 24.
supporting_evidence: The Samaritan canon is limited to the Pentateuch.
No Samaritan textual witness exists for Samuel-Kings.
weaknesses: Not applicable—theory cannot be tested against this passage.

overall_assessment: The numerical divergences in 2 Samuel 24 are best explained by a combination of independent Hebrew textual traditions behind MT Samuel, the Chronicler's Vorlage, and LXX Kingdoms (Cross/Ulrich/Tov), compounded by routine scribal instability in large numerals and at least one demonstrable LXX harmonization (7→3 years of famine toward Chronicles). No single mechanism accounts for every variant, and no systematic mathematical scheme links the figures. The chapter illustrates that Samuel-Kings numerical transmission is fundamentally different from the structured Genesis 5/11 chronologies: it is messy, multidirectional, and reflects the pluriform state of the Hebrew text in the late Second Temple period rather than ideologically driven inflation or deflation.
overall_plain: The differing numbers in 2 Samuel 24 don't follow any neat pattern. They mostly come from multiple ancient Hebrew copies of Samuel circulating with different figures, ordinary scribal mistakes with big numbers, and the Greek translators occasionally smoothing things to match Chronicles.

bibcrit_assessment.title: Pluriform Samuel, not systematic ideological scheme
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: Unlike the patriarchal chronologies of Genesis 5 and 11, where MT/LXX/SP differ along recognizable arithmetic axes, 2 Samuel 24 exhibits the chaotic, multidirectional numerical fluidity typical of Samuel-Kings transmission. The most important implication is methodological: scholars cannot import conclusions from the Genesis chronology debates into narrative-book numerics, because the transmission histories are categorically distinct, with Samuel showing genuine textual pluriformity confirmed by 4QSam-a.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: The differences here look like normal copying noise across multiple ancient editions of Samuel, not a deliberate scheme. That means we shouldn't expect the same kind of explanation that works for the long lifespans in Genesis to apply to numbers in the historical books.
